claim: Optogenetic activation of dorsal striatum dopamine neuron terminals pauses the firing of cholinergic interneurons in both the medial and lateral subregions.
source: With train photostimulation of DA neuron terminals, mimicking the phasic firing of DA neurons (five 5-msec pulses at 20 Hz), mdStr ChIs showed the previously reported pause in firing (Chuhma et al., 2014; Straub et al., 2014), while ldStr ChIs showed a shorter pause in firing followed by an increase in firing (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing firing responses to optogenetic stimulation in both regions, and referenced to Figure 1B showing the pause in firing.

claim: In the lateral dorsal striatum, the pause in cholinergic interneuron firing is shorter due to a subsequent excitation.
source: With train photostimulation of DA neuron terminals, mimicking the phasic firing of DA neurons (five 5-msec pulses at 20 Hz), mdStr ChIs showed the previously reported pause in firing (Chuhma et al., 2014; Straub et al., 2014), while ldStr ChIs showed a shorter pause in firing followed by an increase in firing (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing the temporal pattern of firing responses in ldStr ChIs, with citations to previous work on the pause.

claim: The excitation in lateral dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons is mediated mainly by metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1).
source: This excitation is mediated mainly by metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1) and partially by dopamine D1-like receptors coupled to transient receptor potential channel 3 and 7.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing blockade of the excitation with mGluR1 antagonists.

claim: The excitation in lateral dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons is partially mediated by dopamine D1-like receptors coupled to transient receptor potential channel 3 and 7.
source: This excitation is mediated mainly by metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1) and partially by dopamine D1-like receptors coupled to transient receptor potential channel 3 and 7.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing partial blockade with D1 antagonists and TrpC channel blockers.

claim: DA neurons do not signal to spiny projection neurons in the medial dorsal striatum.
source: DA neurons do not signal to spiny projection neurons in the medial dStr, while they elicit ionotropic glutamate responses in the lateral dStr.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing absence of glutamate EPSCs in mdStr SPNs.

claim: DA neurons elicit ionotropic glutamate responses in spiny projection neurons in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: DA neurons do not signal to spiny projection neurons in the medial dStr, while they elicit ionotropic glutamate responses in the lateral dStr.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing fast glutamate EPSCs in ldStr SPNs.

claim: The DA neurons mediating excitatory signals in the lateral dorsal striatum are in the substantia nigra (SN).
source: The DA neurons mediating these excitatory signals are in the substantia nigra (SN).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing experiments showing that glutamatergic DA neurons projecting to ldStr are located in the SN.

claim: SN dopamine neurons engage different receptors in different postsynaptic neurons in different dorsal striatum subregions to convey strikingly different signals.
source: Thus, SN dopamine neurons engage different receptors in different postsynaptic neurons in different dStr subregions to convey strikingly different signals.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive experimental data showing differential receptor engagement across cell types and regions.

claim: Medially located ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons project to the ventromedial striatum.
source: Medially located ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons project to the ventromedial Str; more laterally located substantia nigra (SN) DA neurons project to the dorsolateral Str (Haber et al., 2000; Ikemoto, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: More laterally located substantia nigra (SN) DA neurons project to the dorsolateral striatum.
source: Medially located ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons project to the ventromedial Str; more laterally located substantia nigra (SN) DA neurons project to the dorsolateral Str (Haber et al., 2000; Ikemoto, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: DA neuron gene expression profiles identify DA neuron subtypes differentially distributed within the ventral midbrain.
source: DA neuron gene expression profiles identify DA neuron subtypes differentially distributed within the ventral midbrain (Poulin et al., 2014) that likely project differentially to striatal subregions, as well as extrastriatal regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous gene expression study.

claim: DA neuron subtypes likely project differentially to striatal subregions, as well as extrastriatal regions.
source: DA neuron gene expression profiles identify DA neuron subtypes differentially distributed within the ventral midbrain (Poulin et al., 2014) that likely project differentially to striatal subregions, as well as extrastriatal regions.
evidence: Based on inference from gene expression data and known anatomical organization.

claim: DA neurons are heterogeneous in their membrane excitability and modulation.
source: DA neurons are heterogeneous in their membrane excitability and modulation (Morales and Margolis, 2017; Roeper, 2013), and the synaptic signals they convey (Chuhma et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on DA neuron properties.

claim: DA neurons are heterogeneous in the synaptic signals they convey.
source: DA neurons are heterogeneous in their membrane excitability and modulation (Morales and Margolis, 2017; Roeper, 2013), and the synaptic signals they convey (Chuhma et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on DA neuron synaptic signaling.

claim: There is significant heterogeneity in DA release and its modulation in different striatum subregions.
source: There is significant heterogeneity in DA release and its modulation in different Str subregions (Sulzer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review on DA release heterogeneity.

claim: DA neurons make fast D2-mediated DA synaptic connections to cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) in the dorsal striatum.
source: DA neurons make fast D2-mediated DA synaptic connections to cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) in the dorsal Str (dStr) (Chuhma et al., 2017), while they elicit slower DA actions via volume transmission throughout the Str (Surmeier et al., 2014; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on DA synaptic connections.

claim: DA neurons elicit slower DA actions via volume transmission throughout the striatum.
source: DA neurons make fast D2-mediated DA synaptic connections to cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) in the dorsal Str (dStr) (Chuhma et al., 2017), while they elicit slower DA actions via volume transmission throughout the Str (Surmeier et al., 2014; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on volume transmission.

claim: In the nucleus accumbens (NAc) medial shell, DA neurons elicit glutamate EPSCs in the three major striatum cell types, with the strongest in ChIs.
source: DA neuron glutamate cotransmission contributes striking regional heterogeneity; in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) medial shell, DA neurons elicit glutamate EPSCs in the three major Str cell types, with the strongest in ChIs (Chuhma et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on glutamate cotransmission in NAc.

claim: In the dorsal striatum, DA neuron glutamate EPSCs have not been seen in ChIs.
source: In the dStr, DA neuron glutamate EPSCs have not been seen in ChIs (Chuhma et al., 2014), while they have been variably observed in dStr spiny projection neurons (SPNs) (Mingote et al., 2015; Stuber et al., 2010; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work, though this is later contradicted by the current study's findings in ldStr.

claim: DA neuron glutamate EPSCs have been variably observed in dorsal striatum spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
source: In the dStr, DA neuron glutamate EPSCs have not been seen in ChIs (Chuhma et al., 2014), while they have been variably observed in dStr spiny projection neurons (SPNs) (Mingote et al., 2015; Stuber et al., 2010; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing variable observations.

claim: The dorsal striatum comprises multiple functional subregions, determined by cortical inputs.
source: The dStr comprises multiple functional subregions, determined by cortical inputs (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Joel and Weiner, 2000; Liljeholm and O'Doherty, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The medial and lateral subregions of the dorsal striatum correspond roughly to associative and sensorimotor striatum, respectively.
source: The medial and lateral subregions correspond roughly to associative and sensorimotor Str, respectively (Joel and Weiner, 2000; Kreitzer, 2009; Liljeholm and O'Doherty, 2012; McGeorge and Faull, 1989; Voorn et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: DA modulates learning and performance of goal-directed behavior in the medial dorsal striatum.
source: DA modulates learning and performance of goal-directed behavior in the medial dStr (mdStr), and formation of habits in the lateral dStr (ldStr) (Faure et al., 2005; Hilário and Costa, 2008; Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: DA modulates formation of habits in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: DA modulates learning and performance of goal-directed behavior in the medial dStr (mdStr), and formation of habits in the lateral dStr (ldStr) (Faure et al., 2005; Hilário and Costa, 2008; Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Studies of functional synaptic connectivity have addressed differences between the NAc and dStr, but not between dStr subregions.
source: Studies of functional synaptic connectivity have addressed differences between the NAc and dStr, but not between dStr subregions.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature showing a gap in knowledge.

claim: ChR2-EYFP is expressed almost exclusively in ventral midbrain DA neurons (over 98%) in DATIREScre;ChR2-EYFP mice.
source: To activate DA neuron terminals impinging on recorded Str neurons, we used mice with DA transporter (DAT) driven channelrhodopsin 2 (ChR2)-enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (EYFP) expression (DATIREScre;ChR2-EYFP mice), in which ChR2-EYFP is expressed almost exclusively in ventral midbrain DA neurons (over 98%) (Mingote et al., 2017), and wide-field photostimulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of the mouse line.

claim: During photostimulation, firing z-scores in the medial dorsal striatum ChIs and lateral dorsal striatum ChIs were both negative, reflecting a reduction in firing, and were not significantly different.
source: During photostimulation, 0–0.4 s from the onset of the train, firing z-scores in the mdStr (−2.5 ± 0.3) and ldStr ChIs (−1.7 ± 0.3) were both negative, reflecting a reduction in firing, and were not significantly different (p=0.074, independent-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing no significant difference.

claim: During the post-stimulation period, firing z-scores in medial dorsal striatum ChIs remained negative, while they became positive in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs, reflecting an increase in firing.
source: During the post-stimulation period, from 0.5 to 0.9 s, firing z-scores in mdStr ChIs remained negative (−2.4 ± 0.4), while they became positive in ldStr ChIs, reflecting an increase in firing (+2.5 ± 0.8) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential post-stimulation responses, referenced to Figure 1D.

claim: Basic membrane properties did not differ significantly between ChIs in the medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Basic membrane properties did not differ significantly between ChIs in the mdStr and ldStr, including baseline firing frequency (mdStr 3.2 ± 0.4 Hz, ldStr: 3.1 ± 0.4 Hz), resting membrane potential(mdStr −62.4 ± 2.0 mV, ldStr −64.6 ± 1.5 mV), action potential threshold (mdStr −50.9 ± 1.8 mV, ldStr −51.8 ± 1.0 mV) and input impedance (mdStr 149.9 ± 15.3 MΩ, ldStr 179.4 ± 18.6 MΩ) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of membrane properties with statistical comparisons.

claim: The peak amplitudes of IPSCs (outward currents) did not differ significantly between medial dorsal striatum ChIs and lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: The peak amplitudes of IPSCs (outward currents) did not differ significantly between mdStr ChIs (23.7 ± 4.5 pA) and ldStr ChIs (18.1 ± 2.8 pA).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with statistical comparison.

claim: Peak amplitude of slow EPSCs (inward currents) was significantly greater in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs than in medial dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Peak amplitude of slow EPSCs (inward currents) was significantly greater in ldStr ChIs (mdStr 1.8 ± 0.6 pA, ldStr 10.4 ± 1.6 pA) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing significant difference.

claim: The charge transfer of PSCs in medial dorsal striatum ChIs was significantly larger than in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: The charge transfer of PSCs (time integration of PCSs) in mdStr ChIs (11.7 ± 1.5 pC) was significantly larger than in ldStr ChIs (3.0 ± 1.6 pC) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing significant difference.

claim: The shorter firing pause in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs was likely due to shorter IPSCs with the same peak amplitude.
source: These observations suggest that the shorter firing pause in ldStr ChIs was likely due to shorter IPSCs with the same peak amplitude, which were captured more effectively by measuring charge transfer.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing similar IPSC amplitudes but different charge transfer.

claim: Application of the D2-antagonist sulpiride blocked IPSCs in both medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Application of the D2-antagonist sulpiride (10 µM) blocked IPSCs in both mdStr and ldStr ChIs (mdStr pre-drug 20.8 ± 2.9 pA, sulpiride 2.5 ± 0.6 pA; ldStr pre-drug 18.0 ± 3.8 pA, sulpiride 3.7 ± 0.6 pA), confirming D2R-mediation of the IPSCs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing blockade of IPSCs.

claim: After sulpiride application, slow EPSCs became recognizable in both medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum ChIs, but were more prominent in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: After sulpiride application, slow EPSCs became recognizable in both mdStr and ldStr ChIs (mdStr pre-drug 1.5 ± 0.6 pA, sulpiride 4.8 ± 0.7 pA; ldStr pre-drug 9.9 ± 1.5 pA, sulpiride 17.0 ± 2.4 pA), but were more prominent in the ldStr (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing emergence of EPSCs after D2 receptor blockade.

claim: The D2-mediated, sulpiride-sensitive components of PSCs did not differ significantly between medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: While pre-drug PSC charge transfer showed significant subregional differences (mdStr 15.3 ± 2.1 pC, ldStr 1.6 ± 3.2 pC), D2-mediated, sulpiride-sensitive components did not (mdStr 17.2 ± 2.1 pC, ldStr 15.8 ± 2.4 pC) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing sulpiride-sensitive components.

claim: DA release in the medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum measured by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry did not differ significantly with single-pulse photostimulation.
source: DA release in the mdStr and ldStr measured by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) (Figure 2D) did not differ significantly with single-pulse photostimulation (mdStr 0.49 ± 0.07 µM, ldStr 0.51 ± 0.07 µM), with train-pulse stimulation (mdStr 0.66 ± 0.09 µM, ldStr 0.64 ± 0.13 µM) (Figure 2E), decay time constant of single-stimulation responses (mdStr 0.29 ± 0.04 s, ldStr 0.31 ± 0.05 s), or of train-stimulation responses (mdStr 0.33 ± 0.03 s, ldStr 0.36 ± 0.05 s) (Figure 2F), or the train/single ratio (mdStr 1.36 ± 0.09, ldStr 1.23 ± 0.09) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by FSCV measurements showing no regional differences in DA release.

claim: The regional differences of PSCs were not due to differences in D2R responsivity or DA release, but rather to a slow EPSC revealed by sulpiride application.
source: Thus, the regional differences of PSCs were not due to differences in D2R responsivity or DA release, but rather to a slow EPSC revealed by sulpiride application.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing similar D2 responses and DA release but different EPSCs.

claim: In lateral dorsal striatum ChIs, slow EPSCs were not blocked by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) antagonists (CNQX and APV).
source: In ldStr ChIs, slow EPSCs were not blocked by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) antagonists (40 µM CNQX and 100 µM APV), while small fast EPSCs were blocked (slow EPSCs pre-drug 14.2 ± 1.8 pA, CNQX + APV 14.3 ± 2.5 pA; fast EPSCs pre-drug 8.9 ± 2.4 pA, CNQX + APV 1.2 ± 0.1 pA) (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing selective blockade of fast but not slow EPSCs.

claim: Small fast EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs were blocked by ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists.
source: In ldStr ChIs, slow EPSCs were not blocked by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) antagonists (40 µM CNQX and 100 µM APV), while small fast EPSCs were blocked (slow EPSCs pre-drug 14.2 ± 1.8 pA, CNQX + APV 14.3 ± 2.5 pA; fast EPSCs pre-drug 8.9 ± 2.4 pA, CNQX + APV 1.2 ± 0.1 pA) (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing blockade of fast EPSCs.

claim: After blockade of D2Rs and iGluRs, small fast IPSCs were revealed in some lateral dorsal striatum ChI cells, which were blocked by the GABAA antagonist SR95531.
source: After blockade of D2Rs and iGluRs, small fast IPSCs were revealed in some cells, which were blocked by the GABAA antagonist SR95531 (gabazine, 10 µM) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing GABAA-mediated IPSCs.

claim: GABAA responses in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs are likely due to DA neuron GABA cotransmission.
source: These GABAA responses, likely due to DA neuron GABA cotransmission (Straub et al., 2014), were not prominent when holding at −70 mV, close to the Cl- reversal potential.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental conditions and citation to previous work on GABA cotransmission.

claim: Slow EPSCs mediated by an unidentified mechanism were responsible for the delayed increase of firing in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs with train stimulation.
source: These slow EPSCs, previously reported by Straub et al. (Straub et al., 2014), mediated by an unidentified mechanism, were responsible for the delayed increase of firing in ldStr ChIs with train stimulation (Figure 2J).
evidence: Based on experimental data showing persistence of firing increase after blockade of known receptors, with citation to previous work.

claim: Regional differences in DA neuron synaptic actions between the medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum were due to slow EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs, mediated by unknown receptors.
source: Thus, regional differences in DA neuron synaptic actions between the mdStr and ldStr were due to slow EPSCs in ldStr ChIs, mediated by unknown receptors.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing differential responses and incomplete identification of mediators at this point in the manuscript.

claim: Slow EPSCs were evoked by single pulse photostimulation at 0.1 Hz and pharmacologically isolated with a cocktail of D2, iGluR and GABAA antagonists.
source: Slow EPSCs were evoked by single pulse photostimulation at 0.1 Hz, pharmacologically isolated with a cocktail of D2, iGluR and GABAA antagonists, and charge transfer measured in the window from 0.2 to 1.7 s after the onset of photostimulation, corresponding to the duration of the EPSC.
evidence: Describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: Single photostimulation evoked small or no slow EPSCs in medial dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Single photostimulation evoked small or no slow EPSCs in mdStr ChIs (2.1 ± 0.5 pC), prominent slow EPSCs in the ldStr ChIs (25.8 ± 4.4 pC), and no PSCs in SPNs in either the mdStr or ldStr (mdStr SPN 0.93 ± 0.24 pC, ldStr SPN 0.64 ± 0.15 pC) (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of slow EPSCs across cell types and regions.

claim: Single photostimulation evoked prominent slow EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Single photostimulation evoked small or no slow EPSCs in mdStr ChIs (2.1 ± 0.5 pC), prominent slow EPSCs in the ldStr ChIs (25.8 ± 4.4 pC), and no PSCs in SPNs in either the mdStr or ldStr (mdStr SPN 0.93 ± 0.24 pC, ldStr SPN 0.64 ± 0.15 pC) (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing large slow EPSCs in ldStr ChIs.

claim: Single photostimulation evoked no PSCs in SPNs in either the medial dorsal striatum or lateral dorsal striatum when slow EPSCs were isolated.
source: Single photostimulation evoked small or no slow EPSCs in mdStr ChIs (2.1 ± 0.5 pC), prominent slow EPSCs in the ldStr ChIs (25.8 ± 4.4 pC), and no PSCs in SPNs in either the mdStr or ldStr (mdStr SPN 0.93 ± 0.24 pC, ldStr SPN 0.64 ± 0.15 pC) (Figure 3A, B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing absence of slow EPSCs in SPNs.

claim: Lateral dorsal striatum ChIs showed significantly larger slow EPSC responses than SPNs or medial dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Charge transfer was significantly different between cell types, between regions, with a significant cell type by region interaction. ldStr ChIs showed significantly larger responses than SPNs or mdStr ChIs.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Medial dorsal striatum ChIs showed significantly larger slow EPSC responses than SPNs, in either the medial dorsal striatum or lateral dorsal striatum.
source: mdStr ChIs showed significantly larger responses than SPNs, in either the mdStr or ldStr.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: No significant difference in slow EPSC charge transfer was observed between medial dorsal striatum SPNs and lateral dorsal striatum SPNs.
source: No significant difference was observed between mdStr SPNs and ldStr SPNs.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Slow EPSCs were not seen in either direct-pathway SPNs or indirect-pathway SPNs.
source: When SPNs were split into dSPNs and iSPNs, there were no differences in charge transfer between region or cell type (Figure 3D); slow EPSCs were not seen in either dSPNs or iSPNs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing absence of slow EPSCs in both SPN subtypes.

claim: Slow EPSCs were exclusive to ChIs and prominent in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Thus, slow EPSCs were exclusive to ChIs and prominent in ldStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing cell type and regional specificity.

claim: Application of TTX blocked slow EPSCs completely, confirming the slow EPSCs were action-potential dependent.
source: Application of TTX blocked slow EPSCs completely (pre-drug 26.7 ± 5.6 pC, TTX 1.2 ± 0.3 pC), confirming the slow EPSCs were action-potential dependent (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing TTX blockade.

claim: Addition of 4AP partially recovered slow EPSCs after TTX blockade, indicating that slow EPSCs have a monosynaptic component.
source: Addition of 4AP partially recovered slow EPSCs (11.3 ± 2.5 pC), indicating that slow EPSCs have a monosynaptic component (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using TTX+4AP to test monosynapticity.

claim: The slow EPSCs are solely monosynaptic.
source: Traces were superimposable after amplitude scaling; the rise time (10% to 90% of peak amplitude) was not different (pre-drug 0.24 ± 0.03 s, TTX + 4 AP 0.21 ± 0.02 s), indicating that the slow EPSCs are solely monosynaptic.
evidence: Based on analysis of EPSC kinetics showing no change in rise time, indicating absence of polysynaptic component.

claim: Slow EPSCs arose from ventral midbrain DA neurons.
source: To confirm that slow EPSCs arose from ventral midbrain DA neurons, we injected a conditional viral vector expressing ChR2 (AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP) into the ventral midbrain of DATIREScre mice and found that the responses did not differ from those recorded in DATIREScre;ChR2-EYFP mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by viral tracing experiments showing similar responses with viral and transgenic ChR2 expression.

claim: Slow EPSCs were almost completely blocked when G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) transduction was blocked by GDPβS in the intracellular solution.
source: When G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) transduction was blocked by GDPβS (0.5–1 mM) in the intracellular solution, slow EPSCs were almost completely blocked 9 min after entering whole cell mode, while EPSCs were not significantly reduced with control intracellular solution (with GTP), showing that the blockade was not due to cell deterioration (comparison to 0–1 min from achieving whole cell, Ctrl 5–6 min 115.2 ± 16.1%, 9–10 min 97.0 ± 15.7%; GDPβS 5–6 min 13.7 ± 8.0%, 9–10 min 6.0 ± 2.9%) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experiments using GDPβS to block G-protein signaling.

claim: Slow EPSCs were GPCR mediated.
source: Thus, slow EPSCs were GPCR mediated.
evidence: Based on inference from the GDPβS blockade experiments.

claim: Bath application of the D1 antagonist SCH23390 significantly reduced slow EPSCs after 20 min.
source: Bath application of the D1 antagonist (antagonist of D1-like receptors) SCH23390 (SCH; 10 µM) or a cocktail of JNJ + MTEP significantly reduced slow EPSCs after 20 min, compared to control (Ctrl) (% pre-drug; Ctrl 95.1 ± 5.4%, SCH 61.4 ± 9.5%, JNJ + MTEP 36.1 ± 5.2%) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing partial blockade with D1 antagonist.

claim: Bath application of a cocktail of JNJ + MTEP (mGluR1/5 antagonists) significantly reduced slow EPSCs after 20 min.
source: Bath application of the D1 antagonist (antagonist of D1-like receptors) SCH23390 (SCH; 10 µM) or a cocktail of JNJ + MTEP significantly reduced slow EPSCs after 20 min, compared to control (Ctrl) (% pre-drug; Ctrl 95.1 ± 5.4%, SCH 61.4 ± 9.5%, JNJ + MTEP 36.1 ± 5.2%) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing partial blockade with mGluR antagonists.

claim: JNJ + MTEP showed significant effects on slow EPSCs after 10 min, while SCH23390 did not.
source: While JNJ + MTEP showed significant effects after 10 min (Ctrl 103.3 ± 2.9%, JNJ + MTEP 50.2 ± 5.3%), SCH did not (SCH 78.7 ± 8.6%), suggesting that longer application was required for SCH action.
evidence: Supported by time-course data showing differential kinetics of antagonist effects.

claim: The slow EPSC reversed to almost pre-drug levels by wash after SCH23390.
source: While JNJ + MTEP effects could not be reversed (44.5 ± 12%), as shown in cerebellum slices (Fukunaga et al., 2007), the slow EPSC reversed to almost pre-drug levels by wash after SCH (95.5 ± 3.8%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reversibility of D1 antagonist effects.

claim: The combined application of SCH + JNJ + MTEP almost completely eliminated the slow EPSC after 20 min.
source: The combined application of SCH + JNJ + MTEP almost completely eliminated the slow EPSC after 20 min (10.1 ± 1.8%) (Figure 5B and C), indicating that slow EPSCs were mediated by mGluR1/5 and D1/5R, but mainly by mGluRs.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing near-complete blockade with combined antagonists.

claim: Slow EPSCs were mediated by mGluR1/5 and D1/5R, but mainly by mGluRs.
source: The combined application of SCH + JNJ + MTEP almost completely eliminated the slow EPSC after 20 min (10.1 ± 1.8%) (Figure 5B and C), indicating that slow EPSCs were mediated by mGluR1/5 and D1/5R, but mainly by mGluRs.
evidence: Based on inference from the pharmacological data showing greater contribution of mGluR antagonists.

claim: With JNJ alone, the inhibition after 20 min application did not differ from JNJ + MTEP.
source: With JNJ alone, the inhibition after 20 min application did not differ from JNJ + MTEP (JNJ 32.8 ± 6.8% pre-drug), while MTEP alone had no significant effect (MTEP 100.6 ± 7.0% pre-drug) (Figure 5D), indicating that the group I mGluR component of the slow EPSC was mGluR1 mediated.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments comparing mGluR1 and mGluR5 antagonists.

claim: MTEP alone had no significant effect on slow EPSCs.
source: With JNJ alone, the inhibition after 20 min application did not differ from JNJ + MTEP (JNJ 32.8 ± 6.8% pre-drug), while MTEP alone had no significant effect (MTEP 100.6 ± 7.0% pre-drug) (Figure 5D), indicating that the group I mGluR component of the slow EPSC was mGluR1 mediated.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing no effect of mGluR5 antagonist alone.

claim: The group I mGluR component of the slow EPSC was mGluR1 mediated.
source: With JNJ alone, the inhibition after 20 min application did not differ from JNJ + MTEP (JNJ 32.8 ± 6.8% pre-drug), while MTEP alone had no significant effect (MTEP 100.6 ± 7.0% pre-drug) (Figure 5D), indicating that the group I mGluR component of the slow EPSC was mGluR1 mediated.
evidence: Based on inference from the differential effects of mGluR1 vs mGluR5 antagonists.

claim: Bath application of mGluR group I agonists have been shown to depolarize dorsal striatum ChIs by activation of transient receptor potential channel (TrpC) 3 and 7.
source: Bath application of mGluR group I agonists have been shown to depolarize dStr ChIs by activation of transient receptor potential channel (TrpC) 3 and 7 (Berg et al., 2007), pointing to TrpC mediation of the slow EPSC.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on mGluR-TrpC coupling in ChIs.

claim: Bath application of the TrpC3 selective antagonist Pyr3 reduced the slow EPSC to 27.2 ± 5.1% pre-drug, without affecting the fast EPSC.
source: Bath application of the TrpC3 selective antagonist Pyr3 (20 µM) reduced the slow EPSC to 27.2 ± 5.1% pre-drug, without affecting the fast EPSC (89.8 ± 12.2%) (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing selective blockade of slow EPSCs.

claim: The TrpC3/7 antagonist flufenamic acid (FFA) blocked the slow EPSC completely, without affecting the fast EPSC.
source: The TrpC3/7 antagonist flufenamic acid (FFA, 100 µM) blocked the slow EPSC completely (3.9 ± 1.1% pre-drug), without affecting the fast EPSC (89.5 ± 4.2% pre-drug) (Figure 6A and B), indicating that the slow EPSCs were mainly TrpC3 mediated.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing complete blockade with TrpC3/7 antagonist.

claim: The slow EPSCs were mainly TrpC3 mediated.
source: The TrpC3/7 antagonist flufenamic acid (FFA, 100 µM) blocked the slow EPSC completely (3.9 ± 1.1% pre-drug), without affecting the fast EPSC (89.5 ± 4.2% pre-drug) (Figure 6A and B), indicating that the slow EPSCs were mainly TrpC3 mediated.
evidence: Based on inference from the differential effects of TrpC3 vs TrpC3/7 antagonists.

claim: Slow EPSCs were mediated by mGluR1 and D1/5R through TrpC3/7 as the effector channel, but mainly by mGluR1 through TrpC3.
source: Taken together, these results show that slow EPSCs were mediated by mGluR1 and D1/5R through TrpC3/7 as the effector channel, but mainly by mGluR1 through TrpC3.
evidence: Based on synthesis of all pharmacological data identifying receptors and channels.

claim: DA neuron glutamate signals are lacking in the medial dorsal striatum.
source: While DA neuron glutamate signals are lacking in the mdStr (Mingote et al., 2015), the mGluR1 component of the slow EPSC in ChIs in the ldStr indicates that DA neuron glutamate cotransmission extends beyond the ventral Str.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and current experimental data.

claim: The mGluR1 component of the slow EPSC in ChIs in the lateral dorsal striatum indicates that DA neuron glutamate cotransmission extends beyond the ventral striatum.
source: While DA neuron glutamate signals are lacking in the mdStr (Mingote et al., 2015), the mGluR1 component of the slow EPSC in ChIs in the ldStr indicates that DA neuron glutamate cotransmission extends beyond the ventral Str.
evidence: Based on inference from the identification of mGluR1-mediated responses in ldStr.

claim: Fast glutamatergic EPSCs have been variably reported in SPNs in the striatum, but without specification of subregion.
source: Indeed, fast glutamatergic EPSCs have been variably reported in SPNs in the Str, but without specification of subregion (Stuber et al., 2010; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing variable observations.

claim: Single pulse stimulation at 0.1 Hz evoked fast EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum direct-pathway SPNs and indirect-pathway SPNs.
source: Single pulse stimulation at 0.1 Hz evoked fast EPSCs in ldStr dSPNs (86.9 ± 12.3 pA) and iSPNs (30.9 ± 5.4 pA), while only small EPSCs were observed in ldStr ChIs (5.9 ± 2.0 pA) (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of fast EPSCs in SPNs.

claim: Only small fast EPSCs were observed in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs when glutamate was isolated.
source: Single pulse stimulation at 0.1 Hz evoked fast EPSCs in ldStr dSPNs (86.9 ± 12.3 pA) and iSPNs (30.9 ± 5.4 pA), while only small EPSCs were observed in ldStr ChIs (5.9 ± 2.0 pA) (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing small fast EPSCs in ChIs.

claim: Fast EPSCs were rarely observed in the medial dorsal striatum regardless of postsynaptic cell type.
source: Fast EPSCs were rarely observed in the mdStr regardless of postsynaptic cell type (dSPN 6.5 ± 2.0 pA, iSPN 3.0 ± 0.4 pA, ChI 8.8 ± 4.3 pA) (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing minimal fast EPSCs in mdStr.

claim: Fast EPSCs in the direct-pathway SPNs and indirect-pathway SPNs were significantly larger in the lateral dorsal striatum than medial dorsal striatum.
source: Fast EPSCs in the dSPNs and iSPNs were significantly larger in the ldStr than mdStr, while regional differences were not observed in ChIs.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Regional differences in fast EPSCs were not observed in ChIs.
source: Fast EPSCs in the dSPNs and iSPNs were significantly larger in the ldStr than mdStr, while regional differences were not observed in ChIs.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The fast EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum SPNs were blocked by CNQX + APV, confirming mediation by ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: The fast EPSCs in ldStr SPNs were blocked by CNQX + APV, confirming mediation by iGluRs (5.7 ± 1.2% pre-drug) (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing blockade with iGluR antagonists.

claim: Fast EPSCs were absent in lateral dorsal striatum SPNs in VGLUT2 conditional knockout mice, but not in controls.
source: To confirm that glutamate responses originated from DA neurons, we examined responses in vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGLUT2) conditional knockout mice (cKO; DATIREScre;ChR2-EYFP;VGLUT2lox/lox) and controls (DATIREScre;ChR2-EYFP;VGLUT2+/+). Fast EPSCs were absent in ldStr SPNs in cKOs, but not in controls (cKO 1.1 ± 0.3 pA, Ctrl 26.1 ± 6.0 pA) (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by genetic manipulation experiments showing loss of fast EPSCs in VGLUT2 cKO.

claim: Slow EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs isolated by a cocktail of D2, GABAA and iGluR antagonists were significantly smaller in VGLUT2 conditional knockout mice, although the responses were not completely eliminated.
source: Slow EPSCs in ldStr ChIs isolated by a cocktail of D2, GABAA and iGluR antagonists were significantly smaller in VGLUT2 cKO mice, although the responses were not completely eliminated (cKO 3.0 ± 0.8 pC, Ctrl 13.7 ± 2.6 pC) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by genetic manipulation experiments showing partial reduction of slow EPSCs in VGLUT2 cKO.

claim: When the D1-antagonist SCH23390 was added to the cocktail of antagonists, slow EPSCs were almost completely abolished, confirming glutamate and D1 mediation.
source: When the D1-antagonist SCH23390 was added to the cocktail of antagonists, slow EPSCs were almost completely abolished, confirming glutamate and D1 mediation (cKO 1.3 ± 0.3 pC, Ctrl 10.2 ± 2.4 pC) (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by combined genetic and pharmacological experiments.

claim: In the lateral dorsal striatum, DA neuron glutamate cotransmission engages different glutamate receptors in different postsynaptic target cells — mGluRs mediating slow EPSCs in ChIs and iGluRs mediating fast EPSCs in SPNs.
source: Thus, in the ldStr, DA neuron glutamate cotransmission engages different glutamate receptors in different postsynaptic target cells — mGluRs mediating slow EPSCs in ChIs and iGluRs mediating fast EPSCs in SPNs; in the mdStr, very little glutamate cotransmission is seen in either ChIs or SPNs.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental data showing differential receptor engagement.

claim: In the medial dorsal striatum, very little glutamate cotransmission is seen in either ChIs or SPNs.
source: Thus, in the ldStr, DA neuron glutamate cotransmission engages different glutamate receptors in different postsynaptic target cells — mGluRs mediating slow EPSCs in ChIs and iGluRs mediating fast EPSCs in SPNs; in the mdStr, very little glutamate cotransmission is seen in either ChIs or SPNs.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental data showing minimal glutamate responses in mdStr.

claim: Based on topography, projections to the lateral dorsal striatum should be from substantia nigra DA neurons.
source: DA neurons project to the Str topographically, with the most medially located VTA neurons projecting to the NAc medial shell and more lateral SN DA neurons projecting to the ldStr (Haber et al., 2000; Ikemoto, 2007). Based on this topography, projections to the ldStr should be from SN DA neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from known anatomical organization cited from previous studies.

claim: In adult mice, VGLUT2 expression is prominent in VTA but not substantia nigra pars compacta DA neurons.
source: However, in adult mice, VGLUT2 expression is prominent in VTA but not SN pars compacta (SNc) DA neurons (Morales and Root, 2014), arguing that non-topographical projections of VTA DA neurons mediate glutamate EPSCs in the ldStr.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous gene expression studies.

claim: With medial dorsal striatum injections of CTB, most DA neurons projecting to the medial dorsal striatum are in the substantia nigra.
source: With mdStr injections, 64 ± 12 cells in the VTA and 323.5 ± 86.5 cells in the SN were CTB+ (Figure 8A, bottom). Among them, 33 ± 8 cells (50.4 ± 3.2% of CTB+) in the VTA and 213 ± 51 cells (66.4 ± 2.8% of CTB+) in the SN were TH+ (Figure 8A, bottom), demonstrating that most DA neurons projecting to the mdStr are in the SN.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing experiments with cell counts.

claim: With lateral dorsal striatum injections of CTB, about the same numbers of DA neurons in the VTA and substantia nigra project to the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: With ldStr injections, 409.7 ± 116.0 cells in the VTA and 223 ± 133 cells in the SN were CTB+. Of these, 242 ± 152 cells (52.5 ± 19.9% of CTB+) in the VTA and 296 ± 88 cells (61.2 ± 23.1% of CTB+) in the SN were TH+ (Figure 8A, bottom), demonstrating that about the same numbers of DA neurons in the VTA and SN project to the ldStr.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing experiments with cell counts.

claim: The distribution of CTB+/TH+ cells in the VTA and substantia nigra differed significantly between medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum injections.
source: The distribution of CTB+/TH+ cells in the VTA and SN differed significantly between mdStr and ldStr injections.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of retrograde tracing data.

claim: There are non-topographical VTA DA neuron projections to the lateral dorsal striatum, but not to the medial dorsal striatum.
source: Thus, there are non-topographical VTA DA neuron projections to the ldStr, but not to the mdStr.
evidence: Based on inference from the retrograde tracing data showing VTA projections to ldStr.

claim: With medial dorsal striatum injections of CAV2-FLEX-ZsGreen in VGLUT2IREScre mice, no ZsGreen+ cells were seen, consistent with the dearth of DA neuron glutamate cotransmission in the medial dorsal striatum.
source: To address this, we injected the conditional retrograde viral tracer canine adenovirus 2 (CAV2)-FLEX-ZsGreen (Ekstrand et al., 2014) into the mdStr or ldStr of VGLUT2IREScre mice to label glutamatergic (VGLUT2+) neurons projecting to the sites injected. With mdStr injections, no ZsGreen+ cells were seen, consistent with the dearth of DA neuron glutamate cotransmission in the mdStr (Figure 8B, middle, left panels).
evidence: Supported by retrograde viral tracing experiments showing absence of glutamatergic projections to mdStr.

claim: With lateral dorsal striatum injections of CAV2-FLEX-ZsGreen, glutamatergic neurons projecting to the lateral dorsal striatum are mostly in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: With ldStr injections, there were 8 ± 4 ZsGreen+ cells in the VTA and 157 ± 13 in the SN (Figure 8B, middle, right panels), demonstrating that glutamatergic neurons projecting to the ldStr are mostly in the SNc.
evidence: Supported by retrograde viral tracing experiments with cell counts.

claim: Among glutamatergic neurons projecting to the lateral dorsal striatum, 24.6 ± 6.8% in the VTA and 57.0 ± 8.5% in the substantia nigra were DA neurons (TH+).
source: Among them, 2 ± 1 cells (24.6 ± 6.8% of ZsGreen+) in the VTA and 90 ± 18 cells (57.0 ± 8.5%) in the SN were DA neurons (TH+) (Figure 8B, bottom).
evidence: Supported by retrograde viral tracing experiments with cell counts and colocalization analysis.

claim: Topographically projecting substantia nigra DA neurons mediate glutamate cotransmission in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Thus, topographically projecting SN DA neurons mediate glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on inference from the retrograde viral tracing data showing SN origin of glutamatergic DA projections.

claim: Variable expression of CAV receptors on DA neuron terminals may have limited the number of DA/glutamate neurons identified.
source: However, variable expression of CAV receptors on DA neuron terminals may have limited the number of DA/glutamate neurons identified.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential technical limitations of the CAV tracing method.

claim: In the substantia nigra, there were 247 ± 11 TH+/ChR2+ and 890 ± 116 TH+/ChR2– neurons, corresponding to 20.7% and 74.8% of all immunopositive neurons, respectively.
source: In the SN, there were 247 ± 11 TH+/ChR2+ and 890 ± 116 TH+/ChR2– neurons (n = 4 animals), corresponding to 20.7% and 74.8% of all immunopositive (TH+ and/or ChR2+) neurons, respectively (Figures 9B and 7C).
evidence: Supported by INTRSECT experiments with cell counts and colocalization analysis.

claim: There were 53 ± 7 TH–/ChR2+ neurons in the substantia nigra, so the specificity of ChR2 expression in DA neurons was 82.5%.
source: There were 53 ± 7 TH–/ChR2+ neurons, so the specificity of ChR2 expression in DA neurons was 82.5%.
evidence: Supported by INTRSECT experiments with cell counts and calculation of specificity.

claim: Of TH+ neurons in the substantia nigra, 22% were ChR2+ indicative of VGLUT2 expression, making them capable of glutamate cotransmission.
source: Of TH+ neurons, 22% were ChR2+ indicative of VGLUT2 expression, making them capable of glutamate cotransmission (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by INTRSECT experiments showing proportion of DA neurons expressing VGLUT2.

claim: Co-labeled terminals (TH+/ChR2+) were denser in the lateral dorsal striatum than in the medial dorsal striatum.
source: Co-labeled terminals were denser in the ldStr, than in the mdStr (Figure 9D).
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations from INTRSECT experiments.

claim: The observation of sparse fibers in the medial dorsal striatum indicated that ZsGreen labeling underestimated the number of DA neurons capable of glutamate cotransmission, because of the small injection volume.
source: The observation of sparse fibers in the mdStr, indicated that ZsGreen labeling underestimated the number of DA neurons capable of glutamate cotransmission, because of the small injection volume.
evidence: Based on inference from comparing INTRSECT and CAV tracing results.

claim: A substantial number of substantia nigra DA neurons express VGLUT2 and project preferentially to the lateral dorsal striatum, coincident with the glutamate cotransmission in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Thus, a substantial number of SN DA neurons express VGLUT2 and project preferentially to the ldStr, coincident with the glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on synthesis of INTRSECT and functional data.

claim: ChAT and VAChT showed high enrichment in ChIs in RiboTag immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Confirming the successful isolation of ChI mRNA, both ChAT and VAChT showed high enrichment in ChIs (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from RiboTag IP experiments showing enrichment of ChI markers.

claim: D5R, TrpC3 and TrpC7 were enriched in ChIs.
source: D5R, TrpC3 and TrpC7 were enriched in ChIs, while mGluR1, mGluR5 and D1R were reduced (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from RiboTag IP experiments showing enrichment.

claim: mGluR1, mGluR5 and D1R were reduced in ChIs relative to whole striatum.
source: D5R, TrpC3 and TrpC7 were enriched in ChIs, while mGluR1, mGluR5 and D1R were reduced (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from RiboTag IP experiments showing reduced expression.

claim: Increased expression of TrpC3/7 and D5R, but not mGluR1, determines the discrete observation of slow EPSCs in ChIs.
source: This suggests that increased expression of TrpC3/7 and D5R, but not mGluR1, determines the discrete observation of slow EPSCs in ChIs.
evidence: Based on inference from the gene expression data showing enrichment patterns.

claim: D1, mGluR5 and TrpC3 expression showed significant differences between the medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: When we compared gene expression relative to GAPDH between the mdStr and ldStr, D1, mGluR5 and TrpC3 expression showed significant differences between the mdStr and ldStr (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing gene expression between regions.

claim: Subregional differences in gene expression were not due to differences in the numbers of ChIs, as their density was the same in the medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Subregional differences in gene expression were not due to differences in the numbers of ChIs, as their density was the same in the mdStr and ldStr (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stereological cell counts showing similar ChI density.

claim: High expression and enrichment of TrpC3 in ChIs appears to be crucial for the slow EPSC.
source: Considering the low expression of D5R and TrpC7 (Figure 10B), reduced expression of D1R in ChIs (Figure 10A) and the minor contribution of D1-like receptors and TrpC7 to the slow EPSC (Figure 4), high expression and enrichment of TrpC3 in ChIs appears to be crucial for the slow EPSC.
evidence: Based on inference from gene expression data and pharmacological results.

claim: The subregional difference in TrpC3 expression between medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum was significantly smaller than the difference in the size of the slow EPSC.
source: However, the subregional difference in TrpC3 expression between mdStr and ldStr was significantly smaller than the difference in the size of the slow EPSC (viz. Figure 3), so differential TrpC3 expression was not the determinant of the prominence of the slow EPSC in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on comparison of gene expression differences and functional differences.

claim: The principal determinant of the medial-lateral difference in slow EPSCs appears to be the projections of VGLUT2+ DA neurons.
source: Thus, the principal determinant of the medial-lateral difference appears to be the projections of VGLUT2+ DA neurons, while the discrete observation of the slow EPSCs in ChIs appears to be due to postsynaptic TrpC3 expression.
evidence: Based on synthesis of anatomical and gene expression data.

claim: The discrete observation of the slow EPSCs in ChIs appears to be due to postsynaptic TrpC3 expression.
source: Thus, the principal determinant of the medial-lateral difference appears to be the projections of VGLUT2+ DA neurons, while the discrete observation of the slow EPSCs in ChIs appears to be due to postsynaptic TrpC3 expression.
evidence: Based on synthesis of gene expression and functional data.

claim: DA neurons differentially control ChIs in the dorsal striatum: they inhibit medial dorsal striatum ChIs, while they inhibit and excite lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: DA neurons differentially control ChIs in the dStr. They inhibit mdStr ChIs, while they inhibit and excite ldStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on synthesis of all experimental data showing differential responses.

claim: The inhibition of ChIs by DA neurons is D2 mediated.
source: The inhibition is D2 mediated, and shorter in ldStr ChIs due to an ensuing slow EPSC.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing D2 receptor mediation.

claim: The inhibition is shorter in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs due to an ensuing slow EPSC.
source: The inhibition is D2 mediated, and shorter in ldStr ChIs due to an ensuing slow EPSC.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental data showing temporal relationship.

claim: The slow EPSC is mediated monosynaptically by glutamate cotransmission activating mGluR1 receptors, coupled to activation of TrpC3/7, along with DA activation of D1-like (D1/5) receptors.
source: The slow EPSC is mediated monosynaptically by glutamate cotransmission activating mGluR1 receptors, coupled to activation of TrpC3/7, along with DA activation of D1-like (D1/5) receptors.
evidence: Based on synthesis of pharmacological and monosynapticity experiments.

claim: mGluR1 responses are observed only in ChIs in the lateral dorsal striatum, while SPNs show iGluR responses.
source: mGluR1 responses are observed only in ChIs in the ldStr, while SPNs show iGluR responses.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental data showing cell type-specific receptor engagement.

claim: Topographic projections of substantia nigra DA neurons to the lateral dorsal striatum mediate the glutamate responses in ChIs.
source: Topographic projections of SN DA neurons to the ldStr mediate the glutamate responses in ChIs.
evidence: Based on synthesis of anatomical tracing and functional data.

claim: Slow DA neuron driven EPSCs are seen discreetly in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs, due presynaptically to substantia nigra DA neuron glutamate cotransmission and postsynaptically to enriched expression of TrpC3.
source: Slow DA neuron driven EPSCs are seen discreetly in ldStr ChIs, due presynaptically to SN DA neuron glutamate cotransmission and postsynaptically to enriched expression of TrpC3, that together determine the unique responses of ldStr ChIs to DA neuron activity (Figure 11).
evidence: Based on synthesis of all experimental data identifying presynaptic and postsynaptic determinants.

claim: Optogenetic activation of DA neurons projecting to the olfactory tubercle evokes a delayed D1-mediated excitation.
source: Optogenetic activation of DA neurons projecting to olfactory tubercle (OT) evokes a delayed D1-mediated excitation (Wieland et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on OT ChI responses.

claim: While the delayed excitation in the olfactory tubercle is solely D1 mediated, D1-like receptors mediate only part of the response in dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: While the delayed excitation in the OT is solely D1 mediated, D1-like receptors mediate only part of the response in dStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on comparison of current findings with cited previous work.

claim: Since DA neuron glutamatergic projections to the medial dorsal striatum are sparse, the small slow EPSCs seen in some medial dorsal striatum ChIs are likely D1R mediated.
source: Since DA neuron glutamatergic projections to the mdStr are sparse, the small slow EPSCs seen in some mdStr ChIs are likely D1R mediated, pointing to slow D1-mediated excitation of ChIs across the Str.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical and functional data.

claim: Both D1 and D5 receptors are expressed in ChIs, but DA application produces the same depolarization in wild type and D1R KO mice.
source: Both D1 and D5 receptors are expressed in ChIs, but DA application produces the same depolarization in wild type and D1R KO mice (Centonze et al., 2003), arguing that the D1 component of slow EPSCs is mainly D5R mediated.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on D1/D5 receptor function.

claim: The D1 component of slow EPSCs is mainly D5R mediated.
source: Both D1 and D5 receptors are expressed in ChIs, but DA application produces the same depolarization in wild type and D1R KO mice (Centonze et al., 2003), arguing that the D1 component of slow EPSCs is mainly D5R mediated.
evidence: Based on inference from cited previous work and current gene expression data.

claim: The slow EPSC in dorsal striatum ChIs is mainly mGluR1 mediated.
source: The slow EPSC in dStr ChIs is mainly mGluR1 mediated.
evidence: Based on synthesis of pharmacological data.

claim: Slow mGluR1 EPSCs were originally described in cerebellar Purkinje cells and ventral midbrain DA neurons.
source: Slow mGluR1 EPSCs were originally described in cerebellar Purkinje cells (Batchelor and Garthwaite, 1997) and ventral midbrain DA neurons (Fiorillo and Williams, 1998; Shen and Johnson, 1997); however, these slow EPSCs are seen only with spike trains, suggesting that they are mediated by glutamate spillover acting at extrasynaptic receptors.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on mGluR1 EPSCs.

claim: Slow mGluR1 EPSCs in cerebellar Purkinje cells and ventral midbrain DA neurons are seen only with spike trains, suggesting that they are mediated by glutamate spillover acting at extrasynaptic receptors.
source: Slow mGluR1 EPSCs were originally described in cerebellar Purkinje cells (Batchelor and Garthwaite, 1997) and ventral midbrain DA neurons (Fiorillo and Williams, 1998; Shen and Johnson, 1997); however, these slow EPSCs are seen only with spike trains, suggesting that they are mediated by glutamate spillover acting at extrasynaptic receptors.
evidence: Based on inference from cited previous work.

claim: Slow EPSCs in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs are reliably evoked with single spikes, at low frequency, suggesting that mGluR1 receptors are closer to synaptic release sites in ChIs than in Purkinje cells or DA neurons.
source: In contrast, slow EPSCs in ldStr ChIs are reliably evoked with single spikes, at low frequency, suggesting that mGluR1 receptors are closer to synaptic release sites in ChIs than in Purkinje cells or DA neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of current findings with previous work.

claim: ChIs, as well as SPNs, express both mGluR1 and iGluRs.
source: ChIs, as well as SPNs, express both mGluR1 and iGluRs, and iGluR responses are evoked in SPNs by stimulation of other glutamate inputs (Ding et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2017), but not mGluR1 responses.
evidence: Supported by current gene expression data and citations to previous functional studies.

claim: iGluR responses are evoked in SPNs by stimulation of other glutamate inputs, but not mGluR1 responses.
source: ChIs, as well as SPNs, express both mGluR1 and iGluRs, and iGluR responses are evoked in SPNs by stimulation of other glutamate inputs (Ding et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2017), but not mGluR1 responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: mGluR1 is not enriched in ChIs.
source: Furthermore, mGluR1 is not enriched in ChIs.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from RiboTag experiments.

claim: The different glutamate responses in ChIs and SPNs — mGluR1 in ChIs and iGluRs in SPNs — appear to depend on the differential distribution of the receptors at postsynaptic sites of DA neuron glutamate cotransmission in the two cell types.
source: Thus, the different glutamate responses in ChIs and SPNs — mGluR1 in ChIs and iGluRs in SPNs — appear to depend on the differential distribution of the receptors at postsynaptic sites of DA neuron glutamate cotransmission in the two cell types.
evidence: Based on inference from gene expression and functional data.

claim: Perfusion of group I mGluR agonists evokes a TrpC3/7 mediated depolarization in dorsal striatum ChIs in rat brain slice.
source: Perfusion of group I mGluR agonists evokes a TrpC3/7 mediated depolarization in dStr ChIs in rat brain slice (Berg et al., 2007); our expression studies show that dStr ChIs express both mGluR1 and TrpC3.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and current gene expression data.

claim: Dorsal striatum ChIs express both mGluR1 and TrpC3.
source: Perfusion of group I mGluR agonists evokes a TrpC3/7 mediated depolarization in dStr ChIs in rat brain slice (Berg et al., 2007); our expression studies show that dStr ChIs express both mGluR1 and TrpC3.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from RiboTag experiments.

claim: TrpC3 is also a major mediator of mGluR1-mediated slow EPSCs in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: TrpC3 is also a major mediator of mGluR1-mediated slow EPSCs in cerebellar Purkinje cells (Hartmann et al., 2008), suggesting that ldStr ChIs share with Purkinje cells the same mGluR EPSC mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on Purkinje cells.

claim: Lateral dorsal striatum ChIs share with Purkinje cells the same mGluR EPSC mechanism.
source: TrpC3 is also a major mediator of mGluR1-mediated slow EPSCs in cerebellar Purkinje cells (Hartmann et al., 2008), suggesting that ldStr ChIs share with Purkinje cells the same mGluR EPSC mechanism.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison with cited previous work.

claim: mGluR1 is also expressed in ventral midbrain DA neurons and their terminals.
source: mGluR1 is also expressed in ventral midbrain DA neurons and their terminals (Fiorillo and Williams, 1998; Zhang and Sulzer, 2004), and presynaptic mGluR1s reduce DA release in the Str (Zhang and Sulzer, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous expression and functional studies.

claim: Presynaptic mGluR1s reduce DA release in the striatum.
source: mGluR1 is also expressed in ventral midbrain DA neurons and their terminals (Fiorillo and Williams, 1998; Zhang and Sulzer, 2004), and presynaptic mGluR1s reduce DA release in the Str (Zhang and Sulzer, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional study.

claim: Since activation of presynaptic receptors requires transmitter spillover, activation of presynaptic mGluR1 on DA neuron terminals by single spikes is less likely.
source: Since activation of presynaptic receptors requires transmitter spillover (Scanziani et al., 1997), activation of presynaptic mGluR1 on DA neuron terminals by single spikes is less likely.
evidence: Based on inference from cited previous work on spillover requirements.

claim: When DA neurons fire in bursts, mGluR1-mediated presynaptic inhibition would limit glutamate cotransmission in the lateral dorsal striatum, and likely reduce temporal summation.
source: However, when DA neurons fire in bursts, mGluR1-mediated presynaptic inhibition would limit glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr, and likely reduce temporal summation.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional consequences of presynaptic mGluR1 activation during burst firing.

claim: While DA neuron cotransmission consistently evokes iGluR EPSCs in the NAc medial shell, reports of EPSCs in the dorsal striatum have varied.
source: While DA neuron cotransmission consistently evokes iGluR EPSCs in the NAc medial shell, reports of EPSCs in the dStr have varied (Chuhma et al., 2014; Mingote et al., 2015; Stuber et al., 2010; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing variable observations.

claim: iGluR EPSCs vary based on recording location in the dorsal striatum, with small or no responses in the medial dorsal striatum and larger responses in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Our present results reveal that iGluR EPSCs vary based on recording location, with small or no responses in the mdStr and larger responses in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on synthesis of current experimental data.

claim: The lateral dorsal striatum — in addition to the NAc medial shell — is a hotspot of DA neuron glutamate cotransmission.
source: Thus, the ldStr — in addition to the NAc medial shell — is a hotspot of DA neuron glutamate cotransmission.
evidence: Based on synthesis of current experimental data showing prominent glutamate responses in ldStr.

claim: Given the topography of DA neuron projections, the lateral dorsal striatum should receive input solely from the substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: Given the topography of DA neuron projections (Haber et al., 2000; Ikemoto, 2007), the ldStr should receive input solely from the SNc.
evidence: Based on inference from cited previous anatomical studies.

claim: CTB results showed the existence of non-topographical projections from VTA DA neurons to the lateral dorsal striatum, as has also been observed in rats.
source: Although our CTB results showed the existence of non-topographical projections from VTA DA neurons to the ldStr, as has also been observed in rats (Maurin et al., 1999; Pennartz et al., 2009), these non-topographical VTA projections do not mediate glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr.
evidence: Supported by current retrograde tracing data and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Non-topographical VTA projections to the lateral dorsal striatum do not mediate glutamate cotransmission in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Although our CTB results showed the existence of non-topographical projections from VTA DA neurons to the ldStr, as has also been observed in rats (Maurin et al., 1999; Pennartz et al., 2009), these non-topographical VTA projections do not mediate glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on inference from comparing CTB and CAV2 tracing results.

claim: Considering the very sparse expression of ZsGreen in the VTA following lateral dorsal striatum injections, the non-topographic projection appears to arise from non-glutamate cotransmitting DA neurons.
source: Considering the very sparse expression of ZsGreen in the VTA following ldStr injections, the non-topographic projection appears to arise from non-glutamate cotransmitting DA neurons, which may contribute to D1- or D2-like receptor responses in ldStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on inference from CAV2 tracing results.

claim: Non-glutamate cotransmitting VTA DA neurons projecting to the lateral dorsal striatum may contribute to D1- or D2-like receptor responses in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Considering the very sparse expression of ZsGreen in the VTA following ldStr injections, the non-topographic projection appears to arise from non-glutamate cotransmitting DA neurons, which may contribute to D1- or D2-like receptor responses in ldStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional role of non-glutamatergic VTA projections.

claim: Retrograde viral tracing showed that most glutamate cotransmission in the lateral dorsal striatum ChIs arises from substantia nigra DA neurons.
source: Our retrograde viral tracing showed that most glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr ChIs arises from SN DA neurons, where VGLUT2 expression has not been reported in adult mice (Morales and Root, 2014).
evidence: Supported by CAV2 tracing data and citation to previous expression studies.

claim: VGLUT2 expression has not been reported in substantia nigra DA neurons in adult mice.
source: Our retrograde viral tracing showed that most glutamate cotransmission in the ldStr ChIs arises from SN DA neurons, where VGLUT2 expression has not been reported in adult mice (Morales and Root, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous expression study.

claim: The discrepancy between current findings and previous reports of VGLUT2 expression could be due to the difficulty of detecting a small population of neurons with relatively low expression levels by in situ hybridization.
source: This discrepancy could be due to the difficulty of detecting a small population of neurons with relatively low expression levels by in situ hybridization.
evidence: Based on speculation about technical limitations of previous methods.

claim: The INTRSECT strategy revealed that about a fifth of substantia nigra DA neurons coexpress VGLUT2.
source: The INTRSECT strategy revealed that about a fifth of SN DA neurons coexpress VGLUT2, which was more than found by in situ hybridization (Morales and Root, 2014) or CAV2-FLEX-ZsGreen retrograde labeling.
evidence: Supported by INTRSECT experimental data and comparison with previous methods.

claim: While DA neurons capable of glutamate cotransmission constitute a minority of substantia nigra neurons, they elicit substantial excitation due to their relatively restricted projection area.
source: While DA neurons capable of glutamate cotransmission constitute a minority of SN neurons, they elicit substantial excitation due to their relatively restricted projection area.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical and functional data.

claim: TH+/VGLUT2+ neurons in the VTA made little contribution to the non-topographic projection to the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: Since TH+/VGLUT2+ neurons in the VTA made little contribution to the non-topographic projection to the ldStr, these coexpressing VTA neurons presumably project topographically to the NAc.
evidence: Based on inference from INTRSECT and CAV2 tracing data.

claim: TH+/VGLUT2+ VTA neurons presumably project topographically to the NAc.
source: Since TH+/VGLUT2+ neurons in the VTA made little contribution to the non-topographic projection to the ldStr, these coexpressing VTA neurons presumably project topographically to the NAc.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical data and known topography.

claim: Retrograde tracing studies revealed that about 40% of medial dorsal striatum or lateral dorsal striatum projecting neurons are non-DAergic, presumably GABA-only or glutamate-only neurons.
source: Our retrograde tracing studies revealed that about 40% of mdStr or ldStr projecting neurons are non-DAergic, presumably GABA-only or glutamate-only neurons (Morales and Root, 2014; Morello and Partanen, 2015).
evidence: Supported by current tracing data and citations to previous characterization studies.

claim: Glutamate-only neurons are seen in both the VTA and substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: Glutamate-only neurons are seen in both the VTA and SNc (Hnasko et al., 2012; Morales and Root, 2014), and indeed we observed 30–40% TH-/VGLUT2+ neurons in both the VTA and the SN (SNc/SNr).
evidence: Supported by current tracing data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Both TH+/VGLUT2+ and TH-/VGLUT2+ (glutamate-only) neurons projecting to the lateral dorsal striatum reside in the substantia nigra, and do not project to the medial dorsal striatum.
source: Both TH+/VGLUT2+ and TH-/VGLUT2+ (glutamate-only) neurons projecting to the ldStr reside in the SN, and do not project to the mdStr, consistent with the recognized segregation of DA neurons projecting to the medial and lateral dStr (Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by current tracing data and citation to previous anatomical study.

claim: Glutamate cotransmitting DA neurons and glutamate-only neurons appear to project similarly to the dorsal striatum.
source: Thus, glutamate cotransmitting DA neurons and glutamate-only neurons appear to project similarly to the dStr.
evidence: Based on inference from the anatomical tracing data.

claim: DA neurons may engage ChIs as a hub to control striatum circuits.
source: DA neurons may engage ChIs as a hub to control Str circuits.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional organization.

claim: Although ChIs comprise only 1–2% of striatal neurons, they exert a strong control of striatal circuits with their large axonal fields.
source: Although ChIs comprise only 1–2% of striatal neurons, they exert a strong control of striatal circuits with their large axonal fields (Kawaguchi et al., 1995; Kreitzer, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: In response to reward-related cues or outcomes, dorsal striatum ChIs frequently show a burst-pause-burst firing pattern, coincident with DA neuron burst firing.
source: In response to reward-related cues or outcomes, dStr ChIs frequently show a burst-pause-burst firing pattern, coincident with DA neuron burst firing (Morris et al., 2004; Schulz and Reynolds, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous in vivo recording studies.

claim: While the early burst in ChI firing is mediated by thalamic inputs, the pause appears to be principally D2R mediated.
source: While the early burst is mediated by thalamic inputs (Ding et al., 2010), the pause appears to be principally D2R mediated.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and current findings on D2 mediation.

claim: The subsequent rebound in ChI firing is highly variable, suggesting that it is generated and modulated independently of the D2-mediated pause.
source: The subsequent rebound in firing is highly variable, suggesting that it is generated and modulated independently of the D2-mediated pause (Schulz and Reynolds, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous in vivo recording study.

claim: Multiple mechanisms likely contribute to the rebound firing in ChIs, one of which is the DA neuron mediated slow EPSC.
source: Multiple mechanisms likely contribute to the rebound firing, one of which is the DA neuron mediated slow EPSC.
evidence: Based on inference from current findings and previous observations.

claim: The presence of the slow EPSC in the lateral dorsal striatum, and not the medial dorsal striatum, likely contributes to subregional variability in ChI rebound firing.
source: The presence of the slow EPSC in the ldStr, and not the mdStr, likely contributes to subregional variability in ChI rebound firing.
evidence: Based on inference from current findings about regional differences.

claim: The slow EPSC is likely to shorten or cancel the D2R mediated firing pause in lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: The slow EPSC is likely to shorten or cancel the D2R mediated firing pause in ldStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on inference from the temporal relationship between the pause and slow EPSC.

claim: Silencing ChIs reduces spontaneous IPSCs in SPNs, while ChI firing increases sIPSCs.
source: Silencing ChIs reduces spontaneous IPSCs in SPNs, while ChI firing increases sIPSCs (de Rover et al., 2002), presumably through activation of a class of GABA interneurons (English et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Cortical or thalamic glutamatergic inputs are reduced by activation of presynaptic muscarinic ACh receptors (mAChR).
source: Cortical or thalamic glutamatergic inputs are reduced by activation of presynaptic muscarinic ACh receptors (mAChR) (Ding et al., 2010; Higley et al., 2009), and a single ChI spike is sufficient to reduce cortical glutamate EPSCs in SPNs (Pakhotin and Bracci, 2007) 391-400).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: A single ChI spike is sufficient to reduce cortical glutamate EPSCs in SPNs.
source: Cortical or thalamic glutamatergic inputs are reduced by activation of presynaptic muscarinic ACh receptors (mAChR) (Ding et al., 2010; Higley et al., 2009), and a single ChI spike is sufficient to reduce cortical glutamate EPSCs in SPNs (Pakhotin and Bracci, 2007) 391-400).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional study.

claim: Pausing ChIs provides a window facilitating excitation of SPNs by lessening GABA inhibition, and simultaneously accentuating glutamate inputs by removing mAChR-mediated inhibition.
source: Thus, we can presume that pausing ChIs provides a window facilitating excitation of SPNs by lessening GABA inhibition, and simultaneously accentuating glutamate inputs by removing mAChR-mediated inhibition.
evidence: Based on inference from cited previous functional studies.

claim: The delayed increase of firing in ChIs caused by the slow EPSCs may regulate the excitation window for SPNs in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: The delayed increase of firing in ChIs caused by the slow EPSCs may regulate the excitation window for SPNs in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional consequences of the slow EPSC.

claim: At a local circuit level, cholinergic tone in the dorsal striatum modifies frequency dependence of DA release.
source: At a local circuit level, cholinergic tone in the dStr modifies frequency dependence of DA release (Threlfell and Cragg, 2011), excitatory input strength, including long-term plasticity (Tanimura et al., 2016), and GABA tone by affecting Str interneurons and SPNs (English et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Cholinergic tone in the dorsal striatum modifies excitatory input strength, including long-term plasticity.
source: At a local circuit level, cholinergic tone in the dStr modifies frequency dependence of DA release (Threlfell and Cragg, 2011), excitatory input strength, including long-term plasticity (Tanimura et al., 2016), and GABA tone by affecting Str interneurons and SPNs (English et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional study.

claim: Cholinergic tone in the dorsal striatum modifies GABA tone by affecting striatum interneurons and SPNs.
source: At a local circuit level, cholinergic tone in the dStr modifies frequency dependence of DA release (Threlfell and Cragg, 2011), excitatory input strength, including long-term plasticity (Tanimura et al., 2016), and GABA tone by affecting Str interneurons and SPNs (English et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous functional study.

claim: DA neuron tonic activity may affect basal cholinergic tone differentially in the medial dorsal striatum and lateral dorsal striatum due to the mGluR component in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: DA neuron tonic activity may affect basal cholinergic tone differentially in the mdStr and ldStr due to the mGluR component in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional consequences of regional differences.

claim: Striatum ChIs play important roles in behavioral flexibility.
source: Str ChIs play important roles in behavioral flexibility (Aoki et al., 2015; Okada et al., 2014); chemogenetic activation of ldStr ChIs enhances switching habits (Aoki et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of lateral dorsal striatum ChIs enhances switching habits.
source: Str ChIs play important roles in behavioral flexibility (Aoki et al., 2015; Okada et al., 2014); chemogenetic activation of ldStr ChIs enhances switching habits (Aoki et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous behavioral study.

claim: The slow EPSC may modulate habit switching by transiently countering tonic DA neuron DA modulation of lateral dorsal striatum ChIs.
source: Therefore, the slow EPSC may modulate habit switching by transiently countering tonic DA neuron DA modulation of ldStr ChIs.
evidence: Based on speculation about behavioral consequences of the slow EPSC.

claim: While DA neurons elicit excitatory signals via D1R and inhibitory signals via D2R across the dorsal striatum, subregional differences in the dorsal striatum involve differences in the strength of the signals.
source: While DA neurons elicit excitatory signals via D1R and inhibitory signals via D2R across the dStr, subregional differences in the dStr involve differences in the strength of the signals.
evidence: Based on synthesis of current findings about regional differences.

claim: Glutamate cotransmission varies in timing and synaptic mechanism, with hotspots of fast cotransmission in the NAc medial shell and lateral dorsal striatum and slow excitation limited to ChIs in the lateral dorsal striatum.
source: In contrast, glutamate cotransmission varies in timing and synaptic mechanism, with hotspots of fast cotransmission in the NAc medial shell and ldStr and slow excitation limited to ChIs in the ldStr.
evidence: Based on synthesis of current findings about glutamate cotransmission.

claim: DA neuron glutamate cotransmission appears to be a major driver of subregional heterogeneity in DA neuron actions across the striatum.
source: Thus, DA neuron glutamate cotransmission appears to be a major driver of subregional heterogeneity in DA neuron actions across the Str.
evidence: Based on synthesis of all findings about regional differences in glutamate cotransmission.
